newsitem.title: CANADA: Agrium-Viridian merger to create fertilizer giant.
newsitem.headline: Agrium-Viridian merger to create fertilizer giant.

text.p: A planned C$1.3 billion ($960 million) merger of Canadian fertiliser makers Agrium Inc. and Viridian Inc. would create an industry giant with sprawling, low-cost operations, company executives said on Monday.

Calgary-based Agrium and Toronto-based Viridian said on Sunday that their boards agreed to a stock swap that would result in an operation valued at C$2.5 billion ($1.9 billion). Under the plan, each share of Viridian would be exchanged for 0.975 share of Agrium.
The deal is the latest in a string of consolidations in the red-hot North American fertiliser industry.

"We have aligned ourselves with a partner that has premium, low-cost productive capacity and (this) will facilitate a new platform for growth in North America, as well as abroad," Agrium Chief Executive John Van Brunt told analysts in a telephone conference call.
Viridian, which has production operations in Fort Saskatchewan and Redwater, Alberta, became a stand-alone fertiliser firm after the split last year of Sherritt Inc.'s Canadian and Cuban operations.
Van Brunt said both firms' shareholders would reap benefits from stronger earnings per share, thanks to more capacity and lower administrative costs, as well as a higher stock price.

The merged firm, which would operate under the Agrium banner, would be North America's largest producer of nitrogen-based agricultural fertilisers, with production and marketing operations in western Canada, Idaho, Nebraska, Texas, California and Argentina.
Analysts saw the new company's access to cheap Canadian natural gas, which is used to produce nitrogen fertiliser, as a major advantage.
The new Agrium would also be a major supplier of phosphate and potash fertilisers.

Viridian Chairman Ian Delaney, who has been a thorn in Washington's side because of his dealings in Cuba with Sherritt International Corp., said his intention was to end his role in the fertiliser industry.
Industry players had speculated that the fertiliser assets were being positioned for a sale since Sherritt Inc. was split in two last year.

The company was separated in a move that allowed Viridian shareholders to be protected from any anti-Cuban-trade moves from the U.S. government. Sherritt was targeted by U.S. sanctions under the Helms-Burton law earlier this year.
With Viridian shares trading on Monday below Agrium's bid value, investors did not appear to expect a competing offer.

Viridian closed up C$1.25 at C$17.75 ($13.15) on the Toronto Stock Exchange. Agrium ended at C$18.55 ($13.75), or C34 cents, also in Toronto and above Viridian when the exchange was factored in. Agrium's shares on the New York Stock exhange ended the day down 25 cents at $13.75.
The companies said the deal included a C$30 million ($22 million) fee that would be paid to Agrium if another suitor outbid it.

CIBC Wood Gundy analyst David Davidson said competing North American companies that would benefit from gaining a larger piece of the continent's nitrogen-based fertiliser business will undoubtedly put the deal under the microscope in coming months.
